Article Title: Billionaire Larry Ellison once struggled to pay his electricity bills to keep his computer running. Now, the Oracle co-founder has written a $300 million cheque to buy a Hawaiian island three times th
Article Text:
How did Larry Ellisonstart with nothing and end up the world’s second-richest man?

A garage startup refused by investors

From unpaid bills to a Hawaiian Island

billionaire Larry Ellison commissioned $400 million Rising Sun yacht in 2007.

Millions spent on floating palaces

Market shocks and technical backlogs

Ellison signed the Giving Pledge in 2010 and promised to give away 95% of his wealth.

Tech billionaire Larry Ellison once struggled so much to pay the utility bills that kept his workshop running that he had to ask energy companies for extra time. Decades later, the business tycoon had no trouble writing a $300 million cheque to buy 98 per cent of a Hawaiian island that is three times the size of San Francisco.The Oracle Corporation co-founder, who is now worth an estimated $256 billion, spent the early years of his career in the 1970s working from a small garage. Money was always tight, forcing him to make a deal with power companies to pay just 10 per cent of his bill upfront so the electricity in his home would not be cut off.For Ellison, keeping the power on had nothing to do with heating, lights, or household comfort. Electricity was essential because it powered his computer, the one machine that stored all of his early software projects."Without electricity, my computer wouldn’t work," Ellison recalled.Ellison's journey to becoming one of the richest people in the world began with an unstable childhood. He was raised by his aunt and uncle in modest circumstances after a difficult adoption and he later dropped out of the University of Chicago.During his early years as an entrepreneur, he spent hours waiting outside the offices of venture capital firms, hoping to secure funding.According to a historical account on Disprz, investors completely ignored his early business pitches.“I couldn’t even get them to say no because nobody even met me!” Ellison said.His fortunes changed after he took a programming job at Ampex, where he worked on a database project for the CIA. The intelligence project had the internal code name "Oracle." Ellison later used that name to launch his own software company with several engineering colleagues.By 2012, Ellison had become wealthy enough to buy 87,000 acres of Lānaʻi, purchasing almost the entire 141-square-mile Hawaiian island for $300 million. The deal effectively made the tech billionaire the main landlord of a community with no traffic lights. Ellison became the owner of the island's only petrol station, its main grocery store, and even its local newspaper.He moved to Lānaʻi full-time in 2020, starting a private plan to turn the island into a 100 per cent green community and a luxury wellness destination.This level of control over an entire island is very different from how Ellison has handled luxury purchases on the mainland. The billionaire once fought a determined two-year legal battle against the city of San Jose just to secure a midnight landing slot for his private jet. Supported by a team of lawyers, he took the case all the way to a US federal court so he could land his $38 million Gulfstream V after the airport's nighttime noise restrictions had begun.Ellison took a very different approach when buying superyachts, often avoiding complex business deals. When he decided to build the Rising Sun, a 454-foot luxury yacht that cost $490 million, he completed the deal without using a single lawyer.Instead, the entire multi-million-pound agreement was completed with famous British designer Jon Bannenberg over a few lattes in London and an exchange of only two emails.Bannenberg created the first designs for the 7,841 gross tonnage yacht in an office that did not use computer-aided design software. Delivered in 2004, the yacht featured a suspended walkway through the engine room so guests could watch the engines running at speeds of 30 knots. It also included a double-height cinema, a wine cellar, a basketball court, a swimming pool, and a private deck reserved only for Ellison.Although the yacht was extended during construction to make it 47 feet longer than Paul Allen's yacht, Octopus, Ellison eventually decided it was too large. He later chose a simpler approach to luxury and sold his remaining share in the yacht to media billionaire David Geffen by 2010.Ellison reduced the size of his fleet by buying the smaller 288-foot Musashi for $130 million. He later admitted that he sometimes regretted selling an even smaller 244-foot yacht called Katana, which his close friend Steve Jobs had once described as being "just about perfect."Ellison's changing luxury lifestyle comes as his personal wealth continues to rise and fall with the stock market. According to Forbes' Real-Time Billionaires List, his net worth recently dropped from about $296 billion to around $249.7 billion in less than a week.The $47.3 billion decline happened because global investors pulled money out of technology and artificial intelligence stocks. Since Ellison owns a 41 per cent stake in Oracle, a 4 per cent fall in the company's share price erased $10.4 billion from his fortune in a single day, pushing him behind Elon Musk, Jeff Bezos, Sergey Brin, and Larry Page in the global billionaire rankings.Despite the sharp fall, Oracle's core business remains extremely strong, supported by the continued growth of its cloud computing operations. Wall Street analysts expect the company to report quarterly earnings of $1.96 per share on revenue of $19.1 billion.Oracle's total order backlog has increased from $553 billion to a projected $661 billion. That backlog is now larger than the total yearly economic output of several small countries, as well as Oracle's own current market value.
Article Summary: Billionaire bought 98 per cent of Hawaiian island for $300 million in 2012. He spent the early years of his career working from a small garage. In 2010 he signed the Giving Pledge to give away 95% of his wealth. He is now worth an estimated $256 billion, according to Forbes.

Article Title: Amazon founder Jeff Bezos' ex-wife MacKenzie Scott once fixed a broken tooth with glue because she couldn't afford a dentist. Now she's giving $20 million to support struggling teenagers' mental healt
Article Text:
Jeff Bezos and Mackenzie Scott

Remembering the weight of poverty before endless fortune

Mackenzie’s Princeton roommate Jeannie Tarkenton loaned her $1000

Driving the early days of Amazon in a borrowed car...

Funding a 'new era' for youth support and mental health

Image – Facebook / Active Minds﻿

Billionaire philanthropist MacKenzie Scott, who once had to fix her own broken tooth with denture glue because she could not afford a dentist, has given a record $20 million donation to a charity working to address the youth mental health crisis in the United States.The donation to the non-profit organization Active Minds is the largest single gift in the charity's history. It comes at a critical time for American teenagers, with data from Fortune showing that nearly one in five adolescents now report having thoughts of self-harm.Scott's donation is enormous compared to the charity's usual finances. Active Minds reported about $9.9 million in annual revenue during the 2025 financial year, meaning this one donation is more than double the amount the organization raised during that year.Now worth an estimated $36 billion according to Forbes, Scott has spent the past seven years giving away an average of almost $10 million every day.Scott's approach to giving is influenced by the financial struggles she experienced when she was younger. While studying at Princeton University, she managed a demanding academic schedule while also working 30 hours a week doing manual jobs.At one point, she was found crying on campus because she feared she would have to leave university after falling $1,000 short of paying her tuition fees.A friend later arranged a loan that allowed her to complete her degree.Her financial hardship also affected her basic healthcare. She once used over-the-counter denture adhesive to hold a broken tooth together because she could not afford treatment. A local dentist later noticed her condition and treated her free of charge.The stress of those difficult years also affected her writing. In a May 1990 letter published in the Princeton Alumni Weekly, Scott thanked her mentor, the famous author Toni Morrison, for giving her "therapy and breathing lessons" while helping her stop worrying so much about revising and finishing her writing.Years after graduating, Scott was still living a modest life as she helped build Amazon with her then-husband, Jeff Bezos. In 1994, Bezos left his high-paying Wall Street job, where he earned the equivalent of $1.5 million to $2 million a year in today's money, to take a chance on the growing internet.Scott fully supported the decision and later said she "couldn't wait to hop in the car." During a five-day trip over the July holiday weekend, the couple drove 2,000 miles across the United States from Texas to Seattle in a borrowed 1988 Chevy Blazer.While Scott drove for most of the journey, Bezos sat in the passenger seat writing the first 30-page draft of Amazon's business plan on his laptop. Using an Excel spreadsheet, he predicted the online bookstore would reach $70 million in sales by 2001. According to journalist Brad Stone, Amazon actually earned more than $3 billion that year.The journey required careful budgeting. When a Motel 6 in Shamrock, Texas, was fully booked, they stayed at a simple roadside motel called the Rambler Motel, where the room was so dirty that Scott refused to remove her shoes.After moving into a garage in Bellevue, Washington, Scott became Amazon's first accountant. She handled the company's bookkeeping, wrote employee paychecks, managed early job interviews, and even negotiated shipping contracts inside a local Barnes and Noble bookstore.Amazon became a public company in 1997 and later grew into a $3 trillion business covering cloud computing, streaming, and artificial intelligence (AI). She got divorced from Bezos in 2019. After that, Scott received a major share of Amazon stock, which she has steadily sold to support charitable causes around the world. She has also faced backlash from billionaires including Tesla CEO Elon Musk for giving away "freebies".The $20 million grant will help Active Minds expand its mental health programs across hundreds of schools and universities in the United States. The Washington, D.C.-based non-profit currently reaches 4.5 million young people through a network of more than 500 student-led chapters.Active Minds said the funding will help create a "new era of mental health" by making support easier to access in local communities and reducing the stigma around mental health challenges."This transformational investment allows us to build a future where every young person knows mental health is a vital part of their overall well-being," the organization said.The charity was created after a personal tragedy. Alison Malmon founded Active Minds while she was a junior at the University of Pennsylvania. Her older brother and only sibling, Brian, developed severe depression and psychosis while studying at Columbia University.Brian kept his worsening condition hidden from friends for years before being diagnosed with schizoaffective disorder. He later died by suicide.Malmon started the organization as a small student group to encourage open conversations about mental health. Financial data from the 2024–25 year shows the charity has grown to include 13,485 official chapter members, with student-led events directly reaching more than 400,000 young people with life-saving suicide prevention information.
Article Summary: Mackenzie Scott has given a record $20 million to a charity working to address the youth mental health crisis in the United States. The donation to the non- profit organization Active Minds is the largest single gift in the charity's history. It comes at a critical time for American teenagers, with data from Fortune showing that nearly one in five adolescents now report having thoughts of self-harm.

Article Title: 'That's what Lindsey wanted': Trump seeks Iran's inclusion in Russia sanctions bill
Article Text:
US President Donald Trump

US President Donald Trump on Sunday backed expanding the proposed Russia sanctions legislation to include Iran, urging Republican lawmakers to broaden the scope of the bill."Republicans should add Iran to the Russian Sanctions Bill. That's what Lindsey wanted to do, and it was going to happen. Important!!!" Trump said in a post on Truth Social.Earlier, Trump had said he "couldn't care less" about Iran's decision to stop abiding by the US-Iran memorandum of understanding (MoU), reiterating that Washington's priority remains preventing Tehran from acquiring a nuclear weapon , according to Al Jazeera.Trump's remarks referred to the "Sanctioning Russia Act", legislation originally championed by the late US Senator Lindsey Graham.A bipartisan group of more than 60 US senators on Thursday (local time) introduced a revised version of the bill, replacing the earlier proposal for blanket tariffs with targeted sanctions aimed at the world's largest buyers of Russian energy.The legislation, titled the "Senator Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia Act of 2026", was introduced by Senators Jeanne Shaheen, Richard Blumenthal and Darline Graham.It seeks to hold major purchasers of Russian oil and gas accountable for supporting Moscow's war in Ukraine.According to the bill's sponsors, Graham met Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy last week and secured White House approval for the revised draft before his death. Graham and Blumenthal had first introduced the sanctions proposal in April 2025.The revised bill "refines tariff authority from a blanket 500 per cent tariff to tariffs on the top five purchasers of Russian crude oil and natural gas of up to 100 per cent," while creating an exception for countries importing less than 15 per cent of Russia's natural gas exports if they are taking significant steps to reduce those imports.The updated legislation also "adds new authority to impose tariffs of up to 100 percent on the top five countries facilitating Russian oil sanctions evasion," "updates the waiver to require a national interest certification consistent with other sanctions laws," "incorporates the bipartisan SHADOW Fleet Sanctions Act targeting Russia's sanctions-evasion fleet," and "includes the bipartisan STOP Russia-China Act targeting Chinese support for Russia's defense industrial base. "Trump had earlier backed the sanctions bill in January, endorsing measures targeting countries that continue to purchase Russian oil.
Article Summary: US President Donald Trump on Sunday backed expanding the proposed Russia sanctions legislation to include Iran. Trump's remarks referred to the "Sanctioning Russia Act", legislation originally championed by the late US Senator Lindsey Graham. A bipartisan group of more than 60 US senators on Thursday introduced a revised version of the bill.

Article Title: After 38 years, DNA test reveals two US men were switched at birth; families sue North Dakota hospital
Article Text:
Kyle Bylin, left and Jeremy Morrison, right/Image : WDAY News

A Christmas gift has led to a life-changing discovery for two families in the United States after DNA testing revealed that two men were accidentally switched at birth nearly four decades ago. The families are now suing a North Dakota hospital, saying they were deprived of the lives they should have shared with their biological relatives.Kyle Bylin and Jeremy Morrison were both born on January 26, 1988, at Unity Medical Centre in Grafton, North Dakota. According to a lawsuit filed last week, they were the only babies born at the hospital that day but were mistakenly sent home with each other's parents, Associated Press reported.The truth came to light after Bylin received an at-home DNA test during a Christmas gift exchange. The results connected him with a biological aunt through a genealogy website, prompting Morrison to take a DNA test. The results confirmed they had been raised by the wrong families.Bylin said he was stunned when the findings emerged, describing the revelation as something he and his family had never imagined. Morrison said he became convinced after seeing a photograph of Bylin's brother, whose resemblance immediately stood out to him.The discovery has left both families grappling with decades of missed milestones. Evelyn Newton, who raised Bylin, said she still considers him her son but feels she was robbed of the chance to watch her biological child grow up."Kyle is still my son. That is never going to change," Newton told AP. She said she can never recover the years she missed, from her son's first steps to learning to drive and getting married.Despite the revelation, Morrison said the DNA results have not changed the way he feels about the parents who raised him."I was loved. I played sports. I did well in school," he said, adding that no DNA test could erase 38 years of memories.Unity Medical Centre acknowledged the impact the discovery has had on the families but said it has found no evidence that hospital staff were responsible for the switch. In a statement, the hospital said: "We recognize the profound impact this discovery has had on them and their families." It added that, because nearly four decades have passed, the medical and staffing records that might have explained what happened no longer exist, and none of the delivery staff from that time are still employed at the hospital.Bylin, however, said he still has the hospital identification bracelet issued at birth, which incorrectly identified him as Kyle Bylin.The two men have since met their biological parents, describing the reunions as emotional but also awkward as everyone adjusts to relationships that should have begun decades earlier. They have spoken to each other by phone but have yet to meet in person.The lawsuit argues that the hospital's alleged error changed the course of two lives and four families, leaving them to come to terms with a truth uncovered almost 38 years too late.
Article Summary: Kyle Bylin and Jeremy Morrison were both born on January 26, 1988, at Unity Medical Centre in Grafton, North Dakota. They were the only babies born at the hospital that day but were mistakenly sent home with each other's parents. DNA testing revealed they had been raised by the wrong families. The families are now suing a North Dakota hospital.

Article Title: Quote of the day: 'Twenty years from now you will be more disappointed by the things that you didn't do' - How this widely loved quote nudges us to choose courage over comfort
Article Text:
Quote of the Day by Mark Twain. (Photo Credit: AI Generated)

Deconstructing the meaning: Regret over risk

Why it resonates, regardless of authorship

"Twenty years from now you will be more disappointed by the things that you didn't do than by the ones you did do. So throw off the bowlines. Sail away from the safe harbor. Catch the trade winds in your sails. Explore. Dream. Discover."This is one of the most widely shared quotes on regret and risk-taking, and it is commonly attributed to Mark Twain, the celebrated American author known for his sharp wit, restless travels, and deep skepticism of a life lived too cautiously. It shows up on posters, graduation cards, and social media feeds around the world, usually presented as timeless wisdom from one of America's most quoted literary figures.A necessary note on accuracy: despite its popularity, quote researchers and Twain scholars have not been able to trace this passage to any of his verified books, letters, notebooks, or recorded speeches. Twain died in 1910, and the earliest known appearances of this exact phrasing surface much later, in 20th-century motivational and self-help literature.It appears to have been attached to his name over time simply because the sentiment fits the adventurous, plain-spoken persona he was known for , Twain did travel extensively, write about exploration, and often mock people who lived too timidly.But the specific words themselves cannot be confidently credited to him. It endures in popular culture today less because of who actually said it, and more because of how precisely it captures a fear nearly everyone recognizes in themselves.At its core, this quote reframes what we should actually be afraid of. Most people hesitate before making a big decision, changing careers, moving to a new city, starting a business, ending a relationship that no longer serves them, because they fear failure, embarrassment, or loss in the short term. The quote flips that fear on its head: it argues the real danger isn't failing at something you attempted, it's never attempting it at all. Failure, in this framing, is temporary and survivable. Regret, left unresolved, tends to compound quietly over the years.The maritime imagery in the quote does a lot of the emotional work. "Throwing off the bowlines" and "sailing away from the safe harbor" cast comfort and routine as a kind of harbor , sheltered, familiar, and safe from storms, but also going nowhere. A ship that never leaves port avoids every wreck, but it also never reaches any destination. The quote suggests that a life spent purely avoiding risk isn't really a full life at all; it's a vessel permanently docked, admired perhaps, but unused for its actual purpose. Looking back decades later, the quote argues, people rarely agonize over the leaps they took that didn't pan out.What haunts them instead is the leap they talked themselves out of, the opportunity they let quietly close, the version of their life they never allowed themselves to test.The words "explore," "dream," and "discover" at the end aren't decorative , they function as a short, deliberate call to action. After painting the picture of the regret that awaits inaction, the quote doesn't linger in warning; it pivots immediately to instruction, almost like a captain giving orders. It's brief on purpose, designed to be remembered and repeated in a moment of hesitation.Even setting aside its uncertain origin, the sentiment behind this quote lines up closely with a well-documented pattern in psychological research on regret. Studies on decision-making consistently find that people tend to regret inaction more than action over the long run. In the moment, human beings are wired to overestimate how painful failure or embarrassment will feel, which pushes many toward the safer, more familiar choice. But that same research shows the sting of a failed attempt tends to fade with time, while the quieter ache of "what if I had tried" often lingers and can even intensify with distance, precisely because there is no closure, no lesson learned, no story to tell , just an open question that never got answered.That may be part of why this quote has had such remarkable staying power despite its shaky sourcing. It isn't popular because a famous novelist supposedly said it; it's popular because it names something a great many people already suspect is true about their own lives, long before they read it in a quote. It gives language to a fear most people carry silently: not the fear of trying and failing, but the fear of one day looking back on a life defined by caution rather than curiosity.The quote has taken on a life of its own , a mirror held up to a very ordinary, very human hesitation. It asks a simple but uncomfortable question: twenty years from now, will you be telling the story of the risk you took, or explaining, still, why you never did.
Article Summary: "Twenty years from now you will be more disappointed by the things that you didn't do than by the ones you did do. So throw off the bowlines. Sail away from the safe harbor. Explore. Dream. Discover" is one of the most widely shared quotes on regret and risk-taking.

Article Title: American woman returns to US after 566 days in Iran on spying charges; Trump thanks Tehran's 'gesture of goodwill'
Article Text:
Dena Karari arrived in San Francisco draped in an American flag. (Photo: X)

Trump announces her departure

Detained after passports seized

Health concerns added urgency

Other Americans remain in Iran

An Iranian-American woman who had been unable to leave Iran for more than a year and a half has returned to the United States after Iranian authorities allowed her to exit the country, prompting US President Donald Trump to describe the move as a "gesture of goodwill. "Dena Karari arrived in San Francisco draped in an American flag, according to a photograph shared by her attorney, Jared Genser, on Saturday."Welcome home Dena Karari from Iran to the land of the free and the home of the brave—after 566 days wrongly detained by the Iranian regime," Genser wrote on X, thanking those involved in securing her return. He also urged continued efforts to secure the release of other Americans still held in Iran.Trump first revealed Karari's departure in a post on Truth Social, saying Iran had allowed an American citizen who was "wrongfully detained" since December 2024 to leave the country."She is now safely outside of Iran, and in good condition," Trump wrote, adding, "The United States of America appreciates this gesture of goodwill by Iran."The White House did not immediately provide further details on the circumstances surrounding her departure.According to Genser, Karari had travelled to Iran to visit family but was prevented from leaving after authorities confiscated both her US and Iranian passports at the airport.A month later, Iranian security officials detained and interrogated her. She was questioned dozens of times and subjected to what her lawyer described as a "coercive exit ban."A source familiar with the case told CNN Karari had been detained, charged, released on bail and barred from leaving the country. Her attorney, however, maintained that she was accused but never formally charged.Karari, 53, worked for a US technology company and also operated the Children of Mehr Foundation, a nonprofit supporting underprivileged children in Iran. Genser said Iranian authorities targeted her over the organisation's activities despite it operating with the required US authorisations.Genser said Karari's deteriorating health made her release especially urgent. He told CNN that she suffered a massive heart attack last week, raising serious concerns about her condition.Calling her return a "minor miracle," he said it was remarkable that she managed to leave Iran amid heightened tensions and military conflict between the US and Iran.The lawyer credited the Trump administration for actively pushing her case during diplomatic contacts with Tehran."They were doing everything they can and pushing from every direction they could," Genser said.Genser said Karari's situation was different from that of other Americans still detained in Iran because her exit ban had expired and she was no longer in prison when she finally left.He urged Iran to drop all remaining charges against individuals associated with the Children of Mehr Foundation and called for the release of all Americans detained or prevented from leaving the country.According to US officials, at least six Americans are currently being held in Iran. Among those designated as wrongfully detained are Reza Valizadeh and Kamran Hekmati.Following Karari's return, advocacy groups expressed hope that her release could pave the way for the freedom of other Americans still in Iranian custody.
Article Summary: Dena Karari arrived in San Francisco draped in an American flag on Saturday. She had been unable to leave Iran for more than a year and a half. US President Donald Trump described the move as a "gesture of goodwill" Karari had travelled to Iran to visit family but was prevented from leaving after passports were seized.

Article Title: Quote of the day by Warren Buffett: “Be fearful when others are greedy, and be greedy when…” - the powerful mindset behind long-term success
Article Text:
Quote of the day by Warren Buffett

“Be fearful when others are greedy, and be greedy when others are fearful.”

Why this idea still matters today

The power of thinking differently from the crowd

What Buffett’s career quietly teaches

Patience creates opportunities: Not every situation requires immediate action.

Knowledge reduces uncertainty: Better understanding leads to better decisions.

Discipline prevents mistakes: Avoiding poor choices can be as valuable as making great ones.

Long-term thinking beats short-term emotions: Temporary market movements should not control important decisions.

How to apply Buffett’s mindset in everyday life

Avoid making decisions only because everyone else is doing it. Popular choices are not always the best choices.

Stay calm during difficult situations. Fear can make people overlook potential opportunities.

Question excitement during successful periods. Confidence should always be balanced with careful thinking.

Focus on long-term goals instead of immediate results. Meaningful success usually takes time.

Learn before making important decisions. Knowledge helps reduce emotional reactions.

Accept that mistakes will happen. The goal is not perfection but avoiding repeated costly errors.

The deeper lesson behind Buffett’s words

Sometimes success is defined by both the choices and the reaction that people have in situations where emotions are in charge. In situations when people experience excitement, they get too confident and make hasty decisions without even thinking about the possible risk. In challenging situations, people act based on fear and miss great chances due to being afraid of uncertainty.However, some of the most successful people in the world have taken a different approach. They try to stay patient, disciplined and wise in their decisions instead of letting emotions control everything.One of the best examples of such an approach is Warren Buffet – one of the most famous investors in the world who became rich exactly because he was able to stay calm while other people were panicking or being too optimistic.The famous phrase from Buffet: "be fearful when others are greedy, and be greedy when others are fearful" is actually the principle of his success. It does not mean that one should do the opposite to what everybody is doing.At first sight, these statements by Buffett can be confusing. How is one supposed to be afraid while other people make money? What does it mean that one should see opportunities while everyone else is scared?The message of the quotation comes from the knowledge about human psychology.Greediness usually leads people to being excessively optimistic and ignoring some possible dangers thinking that prices will rise endlessly. This is why Buffett advises to be careful while feeling such excessive enthusiasm.Fear usually makes people sell out and run away from anything related to what they are afraid of because they think about current issues. In such situations, according to Buffett, there can appear some great opportunities because of people's fearfulness.In simple words, the message says: do not let the crowd's feelings dictate your actions.Markets, businesses and personal decisions are often influenced by emotions. People naturally feel comfortable following the majority because it creates a sense of security. However, history has shown that crowds can sometimes make decisions based on excitement or fear rather than facts.During periods of success, people may assume that good times will continue forever. This can lead to excessive confidence and risky choices. Buffett’s philosophy reminds people to question whether an opportunity is genuinely valuable or simply popular because everyone else is interested.Similarly, during challenging times, fear can create panic. People may make decisions based on temporary uncertainty instead of considering long-term possibilities.The deeper meaning behind Buffett’s message is that emotional control can become a competitive advantage. Those who remain calm and think clearly during extreme situations often see opportunities that others miss.One of Buffett’s greatest strengths has been his ability to avoid herd mentality. Many people make decisions based on what others are doing because following the crowd feels safer.However, Buffett believes successful investing requires independent thinking. If everyone is excited, it may be time to examine risks. If everyone is afraid, it may be time to look deeper and identify opportunities.This does not mean every unpopular decision will succeed. Instead, it means decisions should be based on research, understanding and logic rather than emotions.The lesson extends beyond money. In careers and personal life, people often face pressure to follow trends or make quick choices. Buffett’s philosophy encourages individuals to slow down, evaluate situations and make decisions based on their own judgement.Looking back at Buffett’s decades-long career, one quality stands out: patience.His success did not come from constantly making decisions or chasing every opportunity. Instead, it came from waiting for the right moments and allowing good decisions enough time to grow.Buffett’s approach teaches that:Buffett has often highlighted the importance of reading, learning and improving knowledge. His routine reflects the belief that strong decisions come from preparation rather than impulse.The wisdom behind Buffett’s quote can be applied far beyond investing:The quotation by Warren Buffett, therefore, is all about learning how to control your emotions. In other words, it is important to understand that success is possible only if people manage to remain rational when everyone else is being irrational because of fear and excitement.The biggest benefit is not necessarily having more data and making more decisions. Sometimes, it is just necessary to be patient and observe the situation and make your move once you have the perfect opportunity.It is obvious that Buffett's words show people the truth that long-term success cannot be achieved by reacting quickly. On the contrary, the right decision should be made calmly and logically even when the majority acts differently.Sometimes, when everyone else is acting because of their emotions, this very fact becomes the greatest tool for achieving success.
Article Summary: Buffett’s philosophy encourages individuals to make decisions based on their own judgement. Success is defined by both the choices and the reaction that people have in situations where emotions are in charge. In challenging situations, people act based on fear and miss great chances due to being afraid of uncertainty. Those who remain calm and think clearly during extreme situations often see opportunities that others miss.

Article Title: In the 1800s, an Old World grass likely arrived in settlers’ grain and other cargo, and today cheatgrass fuels larger, more frequent wildfires across the American West
Article Text:
An accidental introduction of cheatgrass reshaped Western landscapes and wildfire cycles. Image Credits: Wikimedia Commons.

How cheatgrass spread across the western United States

That shift has major ecological consequences

Satellite observations and long-term fire records show that grass invasions have contributed to substantial increases in the frequency and size of large wildfires, especially during years with favourable growing conditions. Image Credits: Wikimedia Commons.

Why cheatgrass and wildfire now fuel each other

Mixed unnoticed among sacks of grain carried by European settlers during the late 1800s, the dry, wiry seeds crossed the Atlantic and took root across North America. Few could have predicted that this grass would spread across millions of acres, outcompete native plants, and alter how the American West burns.Today, cheatgrass (Bromus tectorum) is a common invasive species in the western United States. Each year, the grass forms a thick mat of highly flammable vegetation that helps wildfires start more easily, spread faster and occur more often. That, in turn, creates conditions that help cheatgrass spread, reinforcing the cycle. Once cheatgrass takes hold, it is very hard to remove, making it a major ecological problem in the western United States.Cheatgrass is native to Europe, western Asia and parts of North Africa. It arrived in North America during the late nineteenth century, most likely as a contaminant in imported grain, hay, straw and ship ballast brought by settlers. Unlike many native grasses, cheatgrass has traits that help it spread rapidly across disturbed landscapes. The plant germinates in the fall or early spring, often weeks before native vegetation begins growing.By the time many native grasses emerge, cheatgrass has already established an extensive root system, allowing it to capture moisture and nutrients first. It also produces thousands of seeds that can remain in the soil and spread easily by wind, animals, vehicles and human activity.According to the U.S. National Park Service (NPS) , cheatgrass now occupies tens of millions of acres across the western United States and continues expanding into new habitats. The invasive annual grass thrives in disturbed areas such as roadsides, overgrazed rangelands and recently burned landscapes, where it often forms dense stands that crowd out native plants. Its rapid growth comes with another dangerous trait. Unlike many native perennial grasses that remain green well into summer, cheatgrass completes its life cycle early. By late spring or early summer, it dies and dries into a continuous layer of fine, highly combustible material covering the ground.According to research published in the journal Global Change Biology , cheatgrass has fundamentally altered fire regimes across the western United States by increasing the continuity of fine fuels that allow wildfires to spread quickly across landscapes. The researchers found that the invasion has contributed to more frequent fires in ecosystems that historically experienced much longer intervals between burns, creating conditions that increasingly favour cheatgrass over native vegetation.Sagebrush ecosystems have long been at risk. In the absence of cheatgrass, most sagebrush ecosystems used to catch fire only every several decades, some even more rarely than that. With cheatgrass present, fires can become annual events, leaving little time for slower native vegetation to regenerate and giving cheatgrass another chance to thrive. This problem affects more than plants. Wildlife such as greater sage-grouse, pronghorn, mule deer and many insects rely on these plants for habitat.One major challenge in managing cheatgrass is the so-called grass-fire cycle, a self-perpetuating process. When fire sweeps through a region where native shrubs are prevalent, many of those shrubs take years, even decades, to regrow after being burned. Cheatgrass, on the other hand, usually sprouts within days of a fire from its prolific seeds. The following summer, those dense stands dry out into highly flammable fuel that increases the chance of another fire. Each successive fire further reduces native vegetation while creating even better conditions for cheatgrass to spread.According to research published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS) , invasive annual grasses such as cheatgrass have significantly increased wildfire activity across the Great Basin by expanding the amount of continuous fine fuel available to carry fire. Satellite observations and long-term fire records show that grass invasions have contributed to substantial increases in the frequency and size of large wildfires, especially during years with favourable growing conditions.Land managers are using multiple approaches to slow the invasion. These include carefully timed grazing, herbicide applications, reseeding with native species and restoring damaged habitats after wildfires. Researchers are also investigating biological control methods and improved restoration strategies that can help native vegetation compete more effectively against cheatgrass. However, complete eradication remains unrealistic across its enormous range. Instead, most management programmes focus on reducing fuel loads, protecting high-value habitats and preventing new invasions before they become established.Climate change is likely to complicate these efforts. Warming, earlier spring snowmelt, and droughts could allow cheatgrass to thrive while increasing the likelihood of wildfire across most of the Western United States. More than a century after its accidental introduction on settlers’ wheat crops, cheatgrass has become a major invasive species. Over time, cheatgrass has remade whole ecosystems, disrupted the natural wildfire cycle, and changed how wildfires burn millions of acres of western land. Cheatgrass illustrates how a small stowaway can trigger ecological change that lasts for decades.
Article Summary: Cheatgrass (Bromus tectorum) is a common invasive species in the western United States. Each year, the grass forms a thick mat of highly flammable vegetation that helps wildfires start more easily, spread faster and occur more often. That, in turn, creates conditions that help cheatgrass spread, reinforcing the cycle.

Article Title: In the 1930s, South American fire ants likely arrived in Mobile, Alabama, in ship ballast soil, and today their stinging mounds cover much of the US South and cost billions to control
Article Text:
Close-up of a red imported fire ant (Solenopsis invicta), an invasive species known for its painful sting, aggressive behavior and ability to establish large, fast-growing colonies. Image Credits: Wikimedia Commons.

How fire ants invaded the United States

Solenopsis invicta

The economic and ecological cost of fire ants

A colony of red imported fire ants (Solenopsis invicta) swarms across the soil surface, forming densely populated nests that can contain hundreds of thousands of workers. Image Credits: Wikimedia Commons.

A lasting invasive threat

When cargo ships unloaded in the bustling port of Mobile, Alabama, in the late 1930s, little attention was paid to the soil used as ballast. After all, it was merely one of the many components of international business, an efficient method of ensuring stability when travelling across the Atlantic. However, hidden in this ballast was a tiny creature.The reddish-brown ants, native to South America, inadvertently crossed the Atlantic. Once released from the ships, they found Alabama’s climate similar to their native habitat. The lack of natural predators allowed for the rapid growth of the insect population, and they quickly spread from the fields and roadside areas to farms, suburbs and other parts of the community. Almost a hundred years on, those stowaways are now considered harmful invasive species in America. Their painful stings, large mounds and rapid spread have altered parts of the Southern countryside.According to the U.S. Department of Agriculture's National Invasive Species , the red imported fire ant () is native to South America. It is believed to have arrived in the United States through the Port of Mobile, Alabama, in the late 1930s, most likely in soil used as ballast aboard commercial cargo ships.From there, the species spread naturally through mating flights and flooding, while human activities such as transporting nursery plants, sod and soil accelerated its expansion across the southeastern United States. Today, the red imported fire ant is established across much of the southern United States and continues to spread through the accidental movement of infested soil, plants and other agricultural materials.The USDA also notes that preventing the movement of infested materials and colonies remains one of the most effective ways to slow the species' further spread. Red imported fire ants are highly adaptable and thrive in a wide range of environments, particularly areas disturbed by human activity, including lawns, pastures, roadsides, parks and agricultural fields. Their colonies build dome-shaped earthen mounds that may appear harmless until disturbed. When threatened, hundreds of worker ants emerge within seconds, bite the skin to anchor themselves, and then deliver multiple venomous stings. For most people, the stings cause an intense burning sensation followed by itchy, white pustules that can persist for several days. In some cases, individuals may experience severe allergic reactions that require immediate medical attention.The impact of the red imported fire ant extends far beyond painful stings. In agriculture, fire ants damage crops, injure newborn livestock and interfere with harvesting equipment. Their large mounds can blunt mowing machinery, obstruct irrigation systems and reduce the usability of pastureland. Wildlife is also affected, as fire ants prey on ground-nesting birds, reptiles, amphibians and small mammals while competing with native ant species for food and habitat. Urban areas face their own challenges. Fire ants often invade electrical equipment, damaging traffic signals, air-conditioning units, utility boxes and other infrastructure. Schools, parks, golf courses and residential neighbourhoods require regular treatment to keep infestations under control.According to the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) , not only is Solenopsis invicta one of the most studied invasive ants in the world and is listed among five ant species ranked among the world’s 100 worst alien invasive species, but it also estimates that annual spending to control red imported fire ants and repair the damage they cause exceeds US$6 billion.Managing fire ants is difficult because eliminating one mound rarely solves the problem. Colonies can relocate, split or quickly recolonise treated areas. Integrated pest management strategies combine bait insecticides, mound treatments, biological control and careful monitoring, while state and federal agencies enforce quarantines designed to reduce the accidental movement of infested materials.Despite decades of research and control efforts, eradication has not been achieved across the ant's established range. Instead, management focuses on reducing populations and limiting their spread into new regions. The story of the red imported fire ant shows how a routine part of international commerce can have major ecological consequences. The ants arrived unseen in ship ballast soil and have become one of North America’s most difficult invasive species to control. Nearly ninety years after their arrival on the Alabama coast, these unintentional stowaways remain a major ecological force.
Article Summary: The red imported fire ant (Solenopsis invicta) is native to South America. It is believed to have arrived in the United States through the Port of Mobile, Alabama, in the late 1930s, most likely in soil used as ballast aboard commercial cargo ships. Red imported fire ants thrive in a wide range of environments, particularly areas disturbed by human activity. Their colonies build dome-shaped earthen mounds that may appear harmless until disturbed. When threatened, hundreds of worker ants emerge within seconds, bite the skin to anchor themselves, and then deliver multiple venomous stings.

Article Title: Doctors warn of fertility risks after Pentagon orders testosterone tests for troops
Article Text:
US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth (AP image)

Doctors question evidence behind universal screening

Concerns over fertility and other side effects

US defense secretary Pete Hegseth's order mandating testosterone-deficiency screening for all active-duty and reserve service members aged 30 and above has drawn criticism from several medical experts, who question the scientific basis of the policy.Announcing the policy this week, Hegseth said routine screening would help ensure troops maintain optimal hormone levels to improve resilience, endurance and operational effectiveness.However, doctors warn that widespread testing could result in unnecessary treatment and potential health complications.Many specialists say there is little evidence to support routine testosterone testing for all military personnel over 30. Five of the six men's health experts contacted by Reuters said the policy lacks strong scientific backing and could expose healthy individuals to unnecessary medication.Dr Kevin McVary, a urologist and member of Rugiet's medical advisory board, noted that improvements in energy or cognition have mainly been observed in patients who already showed symptoms of testosterone deficiency.Additionly, current recommendations from the American Urological Association and the Endocrine Society advise testosterone therapy only for patients with confirmed hormone deficiency accompanied by symptoms such as fatigue, reduced libido, erectile dysfunction, low bone density or decreased muscle mass.Doctors cautioned that treating people without clear medical indications could amount to overtreatment and expose them to avoidable health risks.Medical experts have also warned that inappropriate testosterone therapy can significantly affect male fertility by reducing the body's natural hormone production, potentially causing testicular shrinkage and impairing sperm production.Other possible side effects include thickened blood, prostate-related issues, acne, hair loss, enlargement of breast tissue, abnormal heart rhythms and mood changes.Experts also pointed to research that prompted the US Food and Drug Administration to remove a previous warning linking testosterone therapy to heart attack and stroke risk.The directive is part of a series of healthcare policy changes under the Trump administration that have generated debate among public health experts.Recent decisions have also included reversing the military's long-standing flu vaccine mandate, later partially reversed after a flu outbreak, and reshaping federal vaccine advisory panels.
Article Summary: US defense secretary Pete Hegseth's order mandating testosterone-deficiency screening for all active-duty and reserve service members aged 30 and above has drawn criticism from several medical experts. Five of the six men's health experts contacted by Reuters said the policy lacks strong scientific backing.

A recent surge in the alleged enforced disappearances of students and young people in Pakistan's Balochistan province has raised fresh concerns over the treatment of those linked to peaceful political organisations. Human rights activist Sammi Deen Baloch expressed her condemnation of the events and alleged that individuals are being taken from their homes, hostels and educational institutions.In a statement posted on X, Baloch described the development as alarming and a part of a broader pattern of enforced disappearances that has persisted in the restive province."The cycle of enforced disappearances in Balochistan has never truly stopped, but over the past few days in particular, there has been an alarmingly dangerous surge in the enforced disappearances of students," she said in a statement posted on X.The activist alleged that the disappearances were being justified as part of counter-insurgency operations, but argued that the approach had failed to bring peace to the restive province. Instead, she said, decades of such policies had deepened resentment and contributed to a cycle of unrest and violence."Abducting unarmed and innocent students, as well as young people affiliated with peaceful political organizations, from their homes, hostels, and educational institutions and forcibly making them disappear, and then justifying this oppression in the name of counter-insurgency, is a failed and inhumane state policy that has been imposed on Balochistan for decades," Baloch said, "If this approach were truly a means to bring peace, Balochistan would not be drowning today in this quagmire of blood, unrest, and hatred; rather, the reality is that this policy is not fostering peace but giving birth to even more hatred and violence.Baloch further alleged that young people were being held for years without being charged or brought before a court, and subjected to torture, humiliation and other forms of mistreatment. Article Title: Pakistan's fifth province? Gilgit-Baltistan assembly passes key resolution amid PoK unrest
Article Text:
Gilgit-Baltistan (AP photo)

Is Pakistan preparing to make Gilgit-Baltistan its fifth province? Amid ongoing unrest in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir, the Gilgit-Baltistan assembly has passed a resolution urging Islamabad to grant the region provisional provincial status, a move that could majorly redefine its administrative structure.The Gilgit-Baltistan assembly on Thursday passed a resolution, backed by both ruling and opposition sides, urging Islamabad to grant the region provisional provincial status, according to Dawn.The resolution, moved by lawmaker Jalal Ali Shah, also sought constitutional and political rights for the people of the mountainous region.Gilgit-Baltistan, located in Pakistan-occupied Kashmir, currently has a semi-provincial administrative status.Pakistan currently has four provinces -- Punjab, Sindh, Balochistan and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. If Islamabad accepts the proposal, Gilgit-Baltistan would become the country's fifth province under a provisional arrangement.
Article Summary: The Gilgit-Baltistan assembly has passed a resolution urging Islamabad to grant the region provisional provincial status. Pakistan currently has four provinces -- Punjab, Sindh, Balochistan and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. If Islamabad accepts the proposal, Gilgit would become the country's fifth province under a provisional arrangement.

Article Title: 'Take off uniform and contest elections': Pakistani MP's open challenge to its military
Article Text:
Pakistani MP challenges their military ( Image quality improved using AI)

Critique on Baloch and Pashtun region

Critique of military

Petition filed against Fazl over remarks

Pakistani politician and chief of Jamiat Ulema-e-Islam-Fazl, Maulana Fazlur Rehman, delivered a blistering critique of Pakistan's military and government, accusing them of failing to maintain order in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Balochistan while warning that the country's Pashtun regions were "drowning in blood.""The country is falling apart. In Khyber Pakhtunkhwa today, there is no government. After the sun sets in the west, until the sun rises in the morning, the police do not step out of their stations. And if the police do not come out of their stations, then the streets will be handed over to armed groups, then the streets and roads will be at the mercy of bandits," Fazl said during a rally Punjab, Pakistan.He directly addressed the military: "I know your authority in my province — you have no government. You are just sitting inside your grand bungalows in the capitals, legs crossed, thinking you are the rulers. At the very least, in my province, you have no government."Fazl said Balochistan had already slipped out of government control and the Pashtun region was now following suit. "In Balochistan, in the Baloch areas, there were rebellions; the entire Baloch region had slipped out of Pakistan's control. Even today, there is no writ of the Pakistan government there.But we were holding back the Baloch region; now the Pashtun region too is drowning in blood."He described the human toll: "In the Pashtun region, within two or three days, we have received more than fifty bodies. All we did in the markets was buy shrouds for our loved ones. All we did was perform funerals for our loved ones."Fazl took aim at military personnel, accusing them of failing to protect citizens despite being paid from public taxes. "Your youth who are becoming martyrs — they have tied the uniform for this very reason, they are taking their salary for this very reason — that they have to fight for the country's security. What favor are you doing me by throwing your blood on me? You are taking your salary from the taxes of my blood and sweat for precisely this. "He added: "I have taken no salary; I will not form any army. You will leave, but you are pushing my homeland toward personal vendettas for generations to come, pushing it toward murder and plunder forever and ever. Explain this politics to someone else; don't try to explain it to us."Fazl challenged the military to enter politics directly. "If you want to do politics, then take off the uniform and come; participate in the elections, and it will become clear what votes people give to those in uniform. It is your prerogative to give government to whomever you want, and to snatch it away from whomever you wish."A petition was filed in a court against Fazl over his remarks, with the petitioner arguing that the speech hurt the sentiments of the general public and caused distress to the families of martyrs. The court sought a reply from the National Counter Terrorism Authority by August 17.Pakistani defence minister Khawaja Asif expressed disappointment, calling Fazl's words "unfair." Pakistan’s planning minister Ahsan Iqbal posted on X: "To describe such an unparalleled sacrifice as merely a compensation for a salary is neither fair, nor in accordance with the demands of ethics, and nor aligned with Islamic teachings."
Article Summary: Pakistani politician Maulana Fazlur Rehman delivered a blistering critique of Pakistan's military and government. He accused them of failing to maintain order in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Balochistan. He warned that the country's Pashtun regions were "drowning in blood"

Article Title: 'Extreme brutality': Pakistan's PTI to launch nationwide protests for Imran Khan's release
Article Text:

The Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf parliamentary party has decided to launch a nationwide movement from August 5 for the release of party chief Imran Khan and acceptance of other demands, a day that will mark the completion of the former prime minister's third year in prison.The decision was made at a meeting chaired by party's interim chairman Barrister Gohar Ali Khan at Khyber Pakhtunkhwa House in Islamabad, where PTI lawmakers discussed parliamentary affairs and the party's strategy going forward.PTI General Secretary Salman Akram Raja told Dawn that the movement would include public meetings, demonstrations and a long march. "It was also decided that Mehmood Khan Achakzai and Allama Raja Nasir Abbas's opinions will be sought for finalising the protest plans and other activities," he said.At a press conference, Gohar said the meeting discussed the health of Imran Khan and his spouse Bushra Bibi. He said August 5 would mark the completion of three years of the PTI founder's imprisonment and rallies would be held across the country to mark the occasion.Khan was arrested on August 5, 2023 after an Islamabad trial court found him guilty of corrupt practices in the Tosha Khana case. He has since been convicted in several cases and remains in solitary confinement at Adiala Jail in Rawalpindi.Raja alleged that Khan had been kept in solitary confinement for months and that no one from his family or lawyers had been allowed to meet him since December last year. "He is not given proper medical care nor is he getting justice from the courts. The oppression and injustice in the country must come to an end," he said.He also warned the government not to launch a crackdown against party workers."Extreme brutality is being carried out here. Imran Khan is being denied meetings with his lawyers, while his sisters are also being barred from seeing him," Raja said as he sat surrounded by party workers outside the jail.Every week, Khan's sisters, lawyers and party workers gather outside Adiala Jail to press the government to allow the family to meet him. On June 14, Khan was taken to a hospital in Islamabad for treatment of his ailing right eye and later shifted back to prison.In a separate development, PTI lawyer Awais Younas Chaudhry submitted a list of six leaders to the Adiala jail administration for a meeting with Imran Khan. The list includes Haji Amanullah Awan, Muhammad Shahid Ali Chahan, Syed Hamid Ihsan, Sajjad Ali Butt, Noman Mughal and Aqsa Hayyat Lali.

Article Title: 'Protection of children is state's responsibility': Pakistan lawmaker seeks social media ban for under-16s
Article Text:
Representative image (AI-generated)

(With PTI inputs)

A lawmaker in Pakistan's Punjab has sought a ban on social media accounts for children under the age of 16 and also called for a similar action across the country.Sarah Ahmad of the Istehkam-e-Pakistan Party (IPP), a partner in the ruling coalition, moved the resolution in the Punjab assembly on Tuesday, marking the first such proposal in any provincial or federal legislature in Pakistan."The protection of children's physical, mental, psychological and moral development is both a constitutional and moral responsibility of the state. Unrestricted access to social media has exposed minors to cyberbullying, online sexual exploitation, inappropriate content, psychological distress, digital addiction and other serious online threats," the resolution said.It urged the federal government to enact legislation "prohibiting children below the age of 16 from creating or maintaining social media accounts unless parental or legal guardian consent is obtained through a reliable age-verification mechanism."The resolution also called on the Pakistan Telecommunication Authority (PTA) to enforce effective age-verification systems across social media platforms operating in the country to ensure compliance with the proposed restrictions.The proposal comes amid growing global efforts to regulate children's use of social media, driven by mounting evidence linking excessive online activity to mental health issues, cyberbullying and exposure to harmful content.Several countries, including Australia and the UK, have introduced age-based restrictions or stronger child online safety measures, while others are considering tougher age-verification requirements for social media platforms.
Article Summary: A lawmaker in Pakistan's Punjab has sought a ban on social media accounts for children under the age of 16. Sarah Ahmad of the Istehkam-e-Pakistan Party (IPP), a partner in the ruling coalition, moved the resolution in the Punjab assembly on Tuesday.

Article Title: Two brothers detained by Pakistani forces found dead in Balochistan; custodial death concerns raised
Article Text:
Imam and Muhammad Umar, two labourers from Mand, were found dead with gunshot wounds after they were allegedly detained by Pakistani security personne

Two brothers who were allegedly taken into custody by Pakistani security personnel were later found dead in Balochistan's Kech district, with their bodies bearing bullet injuries, raising concerns around custodial treatment.The victims, identified as Imam and Muhammad Umar, were residents of Shaban Bazaar in Mand and were reportedly employed as labourers in Jiwani's Kuntani area, according to The Balochistan Post, cited by ANI.The brothers were travelling back to Mand on a motorcycle when they stopped near Balicha Cross after their vehicle reportedly ran out of fuel. Witnesses cited by the publication alleged that security personnel detained the two from the spot.The family later received their bodies through local police. Residents said both men had sustained gunshot wounds.The brothers were laid to rest in their ancestral village of Soro in Mand after funeral prayers. The incident has sparked concern among local residents, who questioned the circumstances leading to their deaths.The report said that before the identities of the deceased became known, several pro-military social media accounts claimed that two suspected militants had been killed during a security operation in the area.However, residents disputed those claims, identifying the deceased as the two labourers and insisting they had no militant links.There has been no official response from Pakistan's military or government regarding the alleged detention or the deaths.Paank, the human rights wing of the Baloch National Movement (BNM), condemned the incident, alleging that the brothers were victims of an extrajudicial killing. The organisation urged authorities to order an independent and transparent investigation and called for accountability if the allegations are proven.
Article Summary: Imam and Muhammad Umar were labourers in Jiwani's Kuntani area. They were travelling back to Mand on a motorcycle when they stopped near Balicha Cross. Witnesses said security personnel detained the two from the spot. The family later received their bodies through local police. Both men had sustained gunshot wounds.

Article Title: LeT, IS operatives among 34 killed in Khuzdar attack: BLA
Article Text:
File photo

In a morale booster for its cadre, Baloch Liberation Army (BLA) has released a statement detailing its massive, coordinated suicide attack on the fortified compound of ISIS-K commander Shafiq Mengal in Pakistan's Khuzdar city last week, claiming to have killed 34 operatives, including terrorists from Lashkar-e-Taiba besides Islamic State In the statement, which stands out for its confident undertone, the rebel group claimed responsibility for the operation - which involved vehicle-borne explosives and a team of suicide bombers - framing it as the official commencement of a broader offensive named "Operation Murg-e-Ghadaran".The attack took place during a gathering at the compound that included Pakistani intelligence officials, operatives from international militant networks, including ISIS and LeT, and former Afghan soldiers, who were reportedly meeting to coordinate efforts against the Baloch political movement, the BLA revealed in its statement. This has yet again exposed the proximity between Pakistan's ISI and Islamic State factions that are being used to quell the Baloch freedom struggle.Falsely accusing India's hand in the incident, Mengal, who survived the attack, said that 17 of his associates, who were having a meal, were killed in an explosion. He said the attackers later engaged in an armed clash with those inside the compound. The assault was executed by BLA's specialised self-sacrificing wing Majeed Brigade.The operation was allegedly set in motion following weeks of strict surveillance by BLA's intelligence wing Zirab, which tracked a high-level meeting.BLA asserted that 34 people killed in the firefight were primary members of Mengal's private network, whom they accused of direct involvement in targeted killings, abductions and enforced disappearances of Baloch political activists and students.
Article Summary: Baloch Liberation Army (BLA) released a statement detailing its massive, coordinated suicide attack on the fortified compound of ISIS-K commander Shafiq Mengal.
